I like data & analyzing data. Part of doing that successfully is that words have very specific meanings for deliberate purposes. I'd like to share a brief glossary of a few key terms used in understanding how "deadly" a disease is. These same concepts apply to just about any cause of death, too.

  1. Mortality Rate
  2. Case Fatality Risk
  3. Infection Fatality Risk
  4. What Can We Do With These Numbers?

Mortality Rate

"How many people in our country die from this each year?"

Mortality rate is the total damage inflicted on a population over a period of time. It is calculated thusly:

deaths / population, where

  • deaths is the total number of people who died from the disease in a given time period
  • population is the total population at the start of the time period

Example

In a country of 1,000,000 people, if 1,000 died in a year (leaving 999,000 at the end of the year), the mortality rate would be

1000 / 1000000, or 0.001 (0.1%)

Case Fatality Risk

"How many of the people diagnosed with the disease go on to die from the disease?"

Case Fatality Risk (CFR) is the proportion of known cases that end up dying from the disease. It is calculated thusly:

deaths / (deaths + recoveries), where

  • deaths is the number of people who were confirmed to have the disease, and also died of the disease
  • recoveries is the number of people who were confirmed to have the disease, and did not die from the disease

CFR may be limited to a specific time period, such as just counting the deaths and recoveries from last year, to see how many diagnosed patients died last year. In that case, you may call it a Case Fatality Rate.

CFR can also be limited to groups of people with specific characteristics, such as "85 years old or older" or "women" or "people who are lactose-intolerant" and for many diseases, CFR can be significantly different for some of those groups. So, just because a disease has "A CFR of 10%" doesn't mean that there's exactly a 1 in 10 chance of death for everyone who gets it.

Example

In a country of 1,000,000 people, if 1,000 people are diagnosed with the disease and then die from the disease and 4,000 are diangosed with the disease but recover, the CFR would be

1000 / (1000 + 4000), or 0.2 (20%)

Infection Fatality Risk

"How many of the people who contract the disease go on to die from the disease?"

It is very uncommon to be able to know that you have identified every single person who contracted a disease. With very-deadly diseases with very unique symptoms (like Ebola or Rabies), this may be possible. For just about everything else, it's pretty much certain that some people will contract the disease and either recover or die without ever going to a doctor and/or getting diagnosed. So, while you might test and identify 5,000 sick people in a year, it may be that 20,000 others had very mild symptoms and never bothered to go to the doctor.

If you were looking at just those 5,000 people to decide how deadly the disease was, it would look much worse!

It's also possible (though less-likely, in my opinion) that you might have missed a bunch of deaths, making the disease look much more mild than it actually is.

Infection Fatality Risk (IFR) is calculated thusly:

estimated deaths / estimated infected, where

  • estimated deaths is an estimate of how many people actually died from the disease
  • estimated infected is an estimate of how many people actually contracted the disease

So how do you get those estimates? Statistical analysis, probably. Different folks will take different approaches to estimate those numbers, depending on their training, opinions, and the data they have available. A common way to do it would be to choose several representative groups of your population and test every single one of them, then autopsy every single one that dies - instead of just looking at numbers from your healthcare system which would usually only include people who were sick enough to seek healthcare.

If you repeat that experiment enough times, you'd get an idea of what the disease's distribution actually was in those populations versus how many showed up through "normal" channels. You can then assume that that's what the disease is actually doing.

If you also have models or predictions of how many people are likely to get infected by a disease, you can combine that with the IFR to get an idea of the mortality rate. If you used the CFR - the "% of diagnosed cases that die" - and applied that % to your model's estimate of how many people would get infected instead of how many people would go and get diagnosed, you might get the mortality rate very, very wrong!

Just like CFR, IFR can also be limited to a period of time, or to a certain demographic - such as the elderly, men, smokers, cat-owners, etc. Also just like CFR, IFR may be quite different among those groups!

Example

In a country of 1,000,000 people, you might take 3 groups of 1,000 people each from a different city, and test every single one of them. It might turn out that in each group of people, 500 had the disease. Of those 500, 50 bothered to go to the doctor for it and get tested, and 10 of those that went to the doctor died. But, of the 450 that didn't bother to go to the doctor, 10 also died from the disease.

The Case Fatality Risk for each of those groups of 1,000 people is

10 / (10 + 40), or 0.2 (20%)

There are 10 deaths and 440 recoveries that didn't get diagnosed, though! In total, that means there were 500 infections and 20 deaths.

The Infection Fatality Risk is then

20 / 500, or 0.04 (4%)

How would this affect attempts to estimate the mortality rate of that disease in our country of 1,000,000 people? For simplicity's sake, let's say that our epidemiologists say that half the population - 500,000 people - is likely to get infected.

If we used the CFR in combination with that, we would say "500,000 people will get infected and 20% will die - that's 100,000 people, or 10% of our country!"

If we did our due diligence, figured out the IFR, and used that instead, we'd say "500,000 people will get infected and 5% will die - that's only 20,000 people, or 2% of our country."

Big difference!

What Do We Do With These Numbers?

Total Damage

Mortality Rate gives you an idea of the total damage a disease will do to a group.

A very deadly disease that infects a small number of the population can have the same mortality rate as a mild disease that infects a huge number of the population. Some Ebola strains kill 90% of their victims, but the US has never had a lot of those Ebola cases - it kills a high percent of a very small number, so the mortality rate is low. In contrast, seasonal flu kills somewhere between 0.06% and 0.1% of its victims (IFR - an estimate)... but is estimated to infect tens of millions of people in the US each year, so its mortality rate is much higher than Ebola.

How Good's Your Healthcare?

Case Fatality Risk shows how successful the medical apparatus is at treating people who get sick.

A disease with a high CFR means that people are getting sick, showing up needing medical care, and the system is failing to save a lot of them.

With a good amount of data, this is probably pretty close to answering "If I catch it, will I die?"

If I get it, will I die?

Infection Fatality Risk is how likely you are to die, if you catch it.

Unfortunately, for new, unknown, or just under-studied diseases, it's hard to get a good estimate of the IFR. Good testing and good data are needed to figure out how many people actually have it and how many people actually die from it. Until those experiments & analyses can be carried out, the CFR is a much easier number to calculate and work with. Inaccuracies in testing or categorizing deaths can skew the CFR up or down - possibly to a large degree!

Typically, you would expect the CFR to stabilize over time and become proportional to the IFR. In just about everywhere with a functional medical system, you would expect the IFR to be lower than the CFR. You just don't know how much lower until larger quantities of quality data get collected.
